_meta.note: Descriptions, scopes, and links are a good-faith summary compiled from each provider's own public materials, not the original agency content. Verify before using for a real planning decision. Entries with url: null could not be confirmed to have a stable current public link.
_meta.coverageRegionNote: coverageRegion values are ids meant to map to GeoJSON files under data/coverage/. Real geometry still needs to be sourced — see data/coverage/SOURCES.md.

tools.name: Adapting to Rising Tides: Bay Shoreline Flood Explorer
tools.description: Maps shoreline flooding as a “total water level” above mean higher high water, combining sea-level rise with storm surge and king tides using county-reviewed, high-resolution data.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable GIS flood-extent layers and a county-by-county methodology report.
tools.slrModel: AECOM Bay Area total-water-level dataset, reviewed by county stakeholders.
strengths: High-resolution, locally reviewed county data
“Total water level” framing separates temporary from permanent flooding
Free, downloadable GIS layers
limitations: Limited to the nine Bay Area counties
Uses today's shoreline, so it doesn't model future erosion or levee change
No built-in population or economic exposure analysis

tools.name: East Contra Costa Shoreline Flood Explorer
tools.description: A companion to the Bay Shoreline Flood Explorer, extending the same total-water-level mapping approach into the Delta-adjacent shoreline of eastern Contra Costa County.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable GIS layers and methodology notes.
tools.slrModel: Extension of the Bay Area total-water-level dataset to Delta conditions.
strengths: Fills a data gap for a Delta-adjacent area other Bay tools skip
Consistent methodology with the Bay-wide Flood Explorer
Locally reviewed data
limitations: Very narrow geography
Same today's-shoreline limitation as the Bay-wide tool
Harder to find now that it isn't centrally indexed — link unverified

tools.name: Sea Level Rise – Coastal Inundation Scenarios (successor to CalFloD-3D Viewer)
tools.scopeLabel: California coast and San Francisco Bay
tools.description: Cal-Adapt's original CalFloD-3D viewer now lives inside the SLR – Coastal Inundation Scenarios tool, which compares two dynamic flood models (CalFloD3D-TFS and CoSMoS) side by side for the same storm and SLR scenario.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable statewide gridded flood datasets at up to 2m resolution.
tools.slrModel: CalFloD3D-TFS and CoSMoS, both funded through California's Fourth Climate Change Assessment.
strengths: Directly compares two independent flood models to show where they agree
Dynamic, time-varying modeling rather than a static “bathtub” fill
High-resolution, downloadable data
limitations: The original CalFloD-3D-only viewer has been folded in, so old links may not resolve
Only two time horizons (2020–2040 and 2080–2100)
More technical interface aimed at modelers than the general public

tools.name: Coastal Risk Screening Tool
tools.description: A quick, address-searchable map showing land projected to fall below various flood or sea-level thresholds — built to give the public a fast, visual sense of local exposure.
tools.reportsData: On-screen summary statistics; limited downloadable data.
tools.slrModel: Elevation-based screening against NOAA tide and flood data.
strengths: Extremely easy for non-experts to use
Covers the whole U.S. coastline, not just California
Good first-pass screening for any one location
limitations: Simplified “bathtub” style mapping, not a dynamic flood model
Not built for detailed infrastructure or economic exposure analysis
Less California-specific detail than the state-built tools

tools.name: Surging Seas Risk Finder
tools.description: Pairs sea-level-rise and flood maps with detailed exposure statistics — population, property value, roads, schools, demographics — searchable by state, county, or place.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable place-level exposure reports and summary tables.
tools.slrModel: NOAA tide-gauge and elevation data combined with Climate Central's flood-threshold modeling.
strengths: Deep exposure analysis by demographic and asset type
Consistent methodology across the whole U.S. coast for regional comparison
Clear, place-level summary reports
limitations: Still largely elevation-based rather than a dynamic hydrodynamic model
National-scale approach can miss California-specific factors like levees
Some layers are coarser than California-built tools

tools.name: Coastal Resilience Evaluation and Siting Tool (CREST)
tools.org: National Fish and Wildlife Federation, with partners
tools.description: Built to help practitioners screen and site nature-based shoreline projects — living shorelines, marsh restoration, dune enhancement — against sea-level-rise and flood exposure.
tools.reportsData: Site-suitability screening outputs for nature-based adaptation projects.
tools.slrModel: Built on state SLR guidance scenarios; exact model not independently confirmed.
strengths: Focused specifically on nature-based / green-infrastructure siting, a gap in most other tools
Brings habitat and marsh-migration data into flood planning
Aimed directly at practitioners, not just the public
limitations: Narrower audience than general-purpose viewers
No stable current link could be confirmed
Less suited to general public education

tools.name: Coastal Flood Exposure Mapper
tools.description: Overlays flood-hazard layers — SLR, storm surge, king tides — with social, economic, and environmental data to show who and what is exposed in a given area.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable maps, data layers, and PDF summary reports by area.
tools.slrModel: NOAA Sea Level Rise and Coastal Flooding Impacts elevation data.
strengths: Broad exposure lens spanning social, economic, and natural-resource data
Consistent NOAA methodology usable statewide or nationwide
Well documented and actively maintained by a federal agency
limitations: National tool, so California-specific nuance like local subsidence is limited
Elevation-based flood layers, not a full dynamic storm model
Interface can feel dense for first-time users

tools.name: Sea Level Rise Viewer
tools.description: NOAA's flagship, slider-based sea-level-rise viewer, showing projected inundation depth, marsh-migration potential, and social/economic overlays for the entire U.S. coastline.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable GIS data and imagery; no per-parcel report generator.
tools.slrModel: NOAA VDatum-based elevation modeling referenced to local tide datums.
strengths: Most widely used and cited U.S. sea-level-rise viewer
Explicitly communicates mapping uncertainty
Includes marsh-migration projections most tools omit
limitations: Does not include beach or dune erosion
Static “bathtub” style mapping rather than dynamic storm modeling
Not California-specific

tools.name: Our Coast, Our Future / CoSMoS
tools.scopeLabel: California coast, including the Bay Area
tools.description: Built on USGS's Coastal Storm Modeling System, this tool dynamically models waves, storm surge, and sea-level rise together to map coastal flooding and erosion at high resolution.
tools.reportsData: Downloadable, high-resolution flood and erosion GIS layers.
tools.slrModel: USGS CoSMoS dynamic wave / surge / SLR model (Barnard et al.).
strengths: One of the few tools that dynamically models waves and erosion, not just static SLR
Very high spatial resolution, down to about 2 meters
Actively maintained by USGS with regular updates
limitations: Heavier, more technical map interface than screening tools
Statewide coverage was built out over years, so some regions arrived later
Large data layers can be slow to load

tools.name: National Flood Hazard Layer
tools.released: Ongoing, effective maps updated on a rolling basis
tools.description: FEMA's official effective flood insurance rate map data, showing regulatory flood zones (e.g. Zone AE, Zone X) and base flood elevations used for insurance and floodplain-management decisions today.
tools.reportsData: Zone lookup and downloadable GIS flood-zone layers via the FEMA Flood Map Service Center.
tools.slrModel: None — reflects today's regulatory floodplain, not a future sea-level-rise scenario.
strengths: The authoritative source for regulatory flood zones and insurance requirements
Public domain, well documented, and continuously maintained by a federal agency
Distinguishes zone subtype and base flood elevation, not just a yes/no flood extent
limitations: Reflects present-day conditions only — no sea-level-rise or future-scenario projections
Zone detail only renders at close-in, neighborhood-level zoom
Coverage and currency of the underlying study vary by county

tools.name: Coastal Resilience Mapping Portal
tools.description: A mapping platform focused on where nature-based solutions — reefs, marshes, dunes — can reduce flood risk, alongside standard SLR and storm-surge hazard layers.
tools.reportsData: Interactive maps and case-study reports; some downloadable data by region.
tools.slrModel: Varies by region and partner project; blends local and national data sources.
strengths: Strong focus on nature-based adaptation options, not just hazard mapping
Long track record with many regional partner projects
Pairs habitat data directly with flood hazard layers
limitations: Coverage and data depth vary a lot by region depending on local partners
Less standardized methodology than a single-model tool
Can lag in areas without an active regional project

tools.name: FloodRISE
tools.description: A UC Irvine research project modeling compound flooding from sea-level rise, storm surge, and inland stormwater runoff together for Orange County's Newport Bay — showing how these hazards interact rather than treating them separately.
tools.reportsData: Academic reports and journal publications; interactive viewer availability has varied.
tools.slrModel: Custom hydrodynamic model developed by UCI researchers, funded by NOAA and Sea Grant.
strengths: Pioneered “compound flooding” analysis combining ocean and stormwater hazards
Strong peer-reviewed academic foundation
Detailed local modeling for a specific vulnerable community
limitations: Very limited geographic coverage (Newport Bay area only)
As a university research project, long-term public hosting isn't guaranteed
No current public tool link could be confirmed

tools.name: Hazard Exposure Reporting and Analytics (HERA)
tools.description: Lets users pick a flood-hazard scenario — SLR plus storm intensity — then generates population, economic, land-cover, and infrastructure exposure dashboards for one community or several side by side.
tools.reportsData: Interactive dashboards plus downloadable community-level exposure datasets.
tools.slrModel: USGS hazard-zone scenarios combining SLR increments with storm categories.
strengths: Strong community-level socioeconomic exposure analysis, not just flood extent
Lets users directly compare exposure across multiple communities
Covers flooding, groundwater, and erosion hazards in one place
limitations: Requires picking a scenario first, which assumes some baseline knowledge
National tool, so hyper-local California factors may be generalized
Dashboard-heavy interface takes more clicks than a simple map
